extracted.intended_audience: Employers, petitioners, immigration attorneys, and stakeholders responding to or implementing the H-1B weighted selection rule
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and procedural criteria governing DHS's implementation of a wage-weighted H-1B registration/selection process, including data sources (OEWS), how wage levels are determined and reported, statutory authority questions, and fairness/administrability concerns raised in notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and Regional Disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters said the weighted selection process fails to account for regional differences in wage levels, creating geographic inequities and favoring employers in high-wage metropolitan areas while disadvantaging those in regions with lower costs of living and correspondingly lower prevailing wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: registrations will be weighted according to the highest OEWS prevailing wage level that the proffered wage equals or exceeds for the area of intended employment; "registrations corresponding to the same wage level will be weighted the same regardless of whether their proffered wages are different owing to their areas of intended employment." The final rule "neutralizes geographic differences in salary amounts by taking into account the area of intended employment when weighting registrations."

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Total Compensation vs. Base Wage
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued the selection process should consider all aspects of compensation (bonuses, equity, benefits, commission, cost-of-living allowance, stock options, etc.), not only base wages, and suggested mechanisms such as valuing stock or using past IRS transcripts to capture total compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: cash bonuses may, in limited circumstances, be counted toward annual salary (see 20 CFR 655.731(c)(2)), but many forms of compensation (stock options, profit sharing, flexible benefits) are not readily quantifiable or guaranteed and thus cannot reliably be calculated into proffered wages. "This rule does not change how wages are defined or measured." DHS believes there is no viable uncomplicated, predictable alternative to using base wages for weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Disadvantage to Startups and Small Businesses (equity-heavy compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters warned that employers relying on equity-based pay, future profit participation, or stock options (common in startups and small businesses) would be disadvantaged if only base salary counts toward selection weighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges varied compensation forms but reiterates inability to incorporate non-cash compensation reliably into weighting; employers remain free to offer higher base wages to increase selection chances, but DHS will not change wage definitions to capture equity or non-guaranteed compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage as Proxy for Skill, Experience, or Education
rubrics_metrics.description: Many commenters said wage is not a proxy for experience, skill, or education and that using wage conflates pay with contribution to the economy or innovation potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS disagrees and states that "salary generally is a reasonable proxy for skill level," citing DOL materials and other sources. DHS's policy goal is to "generally favor the allocation of H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens, while ensuring meaningful opportunities for selection regardless of industry or profession."

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve Opportunities Across Wage Levels (protect early-career, research, academic roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters expressed concern the rule would reduce chances for entrepreneurial, academic, research, early-career professionals and sectors that rely on them, arguing the rule might favor experienced, high-paid workers and big firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: the rule "does not shut out early-career professionals," recognizes it may decrease selection chance for level I wages but maintains that the opportunity to secure H-1B workers at all wage levels is preserved; DHS accepts some trade-offs given the aim to favor higher-skilled/higher-paid workers overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of OEWS Data and Its Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters criticized relying on the OEWS program, arguing OEWS wage data were not intended to measure skill or productivity, aggregate across employers without adjusting for industry/business model/regional factors, and reflect percentiles rather than individualized experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: OEWS represents the best available resource for this purpose because it is already used in the H-1B program, is publicly available, updated annually, familiar to petitioners, and allows USCIS to leverage employers' existing knowledge; if OEWS wage level is unavailable, employers should determine the wage level using DOL guidance they would otherwise follow when selecting the wage level on the LCA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registrants Must Select Highest OEWS Wage Level Matching Proffered Wage
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters worried about confusion between the wage level offered for USCIS registration purposes and the prevailing wage level calculated under DOL rules on the LCA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: a registrant is required to select the box for the highest OEWS wage level that the beneficiary's proffered wage generally equals or exceeds for the relevant SOC code in the area(s) of intended employment. DHS declined to modify 8 CFR 214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1) to discuss DOL prevailing wage calculation because that provision concerns USCIS filing procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural Clarity: Avoid Confusing USCIS Registration vs. DOL Prevailing Wage Calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters urged clarity that the wage level used for USCIS registration/weighting is distinct from the prevailing wage calculation on the LCA and should not create mismatches or confusion during adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: emphasizes registrant selects OEWS wage level based on proffered wage for registration; LCA prevailing wage continues to be governed by DOL rules when submitting the actual petition, and USCIS will not conflate those calculations within its filing-procedure regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Authority and Consistency with INA
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued the proposed weighted selection process violates INA sec. 214(g)(3)'s directive to issue visas in the "order in which petitions are filed" and asserted DHS lacks statutory authority to adopt wage-based prioritization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: the statute is silent/ambiguous as to what it means to "file" and how to order petitions filed in the same timeframe; DHS invokes INA secs. 103(a), 214(a), and (c)(1) as authority to prescribe rules to fill statutory gaps. DHS cites case law and prior practice (e.g., registration requirement, random selection) to justify reasoned gap-filling and concludes weighted selection is within its authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness, Orderly Administration, and Program Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters contended any selection method should be fair, not arbitrary, and consistent with congressional intent; some argued only random selection is permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: selection methods should ensure "a fair, orderly, and efficient allocation" and that pure randomization "does not serve the ends of the H-1B program or congressional intent to help U.S. employers fill labor shortages in positions requiring highly skilled workers." DHS frames weighted selection as a reasonable method to further program goals while filling statutory silence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrability and Predictability (practical implementability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters asked that any weighting system be administrable, not create enforcement disputes at scale (e.g., adjudicating disputes over bonuses/equity), and be uncomplicated and predictable for petitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: selected an approach using familiar, public OEWS wage levels to minimize confusion and administrative burden; DHS acknowledges it cannot account for every rare scenario (e.g., a laid-off level IV worker taking a level II bridge job) and prioritizes an uncomplicated, predictable system even if it cannot capture all edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-discrimination Across Race, Nationality, and Protected Groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters alleged the rule would disproportionately impact certain minority groups (e.g., Asian and Pacific Islander, Hispanic) because of their representation among H-1B workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: the rule does not target or favor any particular minority group; selection is based on wage level without regard to race, ethnicity, or country of origin, and DHS disagrees the rule will deepen racial wealth disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Government Wage Determination / Market Intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: A commenter stated the proposed weighted selection system risks government manipulation of market-based wages and represents a "fundamental departure" from U.S. labor market norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS: rejects the characterization that the rule is government intervention in wages; DHS is not mandating wages, employers remain free to set wages and to choose whether to participate in the H-1B program; existing prevailing-wage requirements have long existed and this rule does not change them.
